name: Demeclocycline
summary: A tetracycline antibiotic that also makes the kidneys excrete free water; nothing links it to facial puffiness.
lead: Demeclocycline is a semisynthetic tetracycline antibiotic used for infections caused by susceptible organisms such as rickettsiae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Chlamydia species. Separately, it blunts the kidney's response to antidiuretic hormone, producing an aquaretic effect that has been used off-label in the syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH).

name: Theobromine
summary: Cocoa's main xanthine, a mild diuretic with no published evidence for de-puffing.
lead: Theobromine is the main alkaloid of the cacao plant (Theobroma cacao) and a dimethylxanthine closely related to caffeine and theophylline. It occurs in cocoa and chocolate, with smaller amounts in tea, yerba mate, kola nut and guarana . Reference works describe it as a mild diuretic, heart stimulant and bronchodilator with much weaker central nervous system stimulation than caffeine .

name: Theophylline
summary: A prescription asthma bronchodilator with diuretic history; nothing tests it for puffiness.
lead: Theophylline (1,3-dimethylxanthine) is a methylxanthine drug that inhibits phosphodiesterases and blocks adenosine receptors. It is prescribed for chronic asthma, COPD and apnea of prematurity, and occurs naturally in small amounts in tea . Its first clinical use, in 1902, was as a diuretic, before it was adopted for asthma about two decades later .

name: Glycopyrrolate (oral)
summary: Prescription anticholinergic pill sometimes used off-label for sweating; evidence for appearance use is thin.
lead: Glycopyrrolate, also called glycopyrronium bromide, is a synthetic quaternary-ammonium muscarinic anticholinergic that acts mainly outside the brain. It is given by mouth, injection, topically or by inhalation and has been used since 1961, first for peptic ulcer .

name: Glycopyrronium tosylate (Qbrexza)
summary: FDA-approved underarm sweat wipe with phase 3 trial support; Rx-only.
lead: Glycopyrronium tosylate is a topical anticholinergic applied as a once-daily cloth to the underarms for primary axillary hyperhidrosis. Sold in the US as Qbrexza (2.4 percent cloth), it was approved by the FDA in June 2018 for people aged 9 and older and in Japan in January 2022 .

name: Propantheline
summary: Older prescription anticholinergic tablet that dermatology sources list for sweating; no sweat trials found.
lead: Propantheline bromide is an oral antimuscarinic drug that blocks acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors in smooth muscle, glands and the eye. Reference works list it for excessive sweating (hyperhidrosis), cramps or spasms of the stomach, intestines or bladder, and involuntary urination; dentists sometimes use it to reduce salivation. A brand name is Pro-Banthine .

name: Aluminum chloride hexahydrate (Drysol)
summary: Prescription-strength antiperspirant salt; guideline first-line for hyperhidrosis, with irritation the main downside.
lead: Aluminium chloride hexahydrate is the active ingredient in prescription-strength antiperspirants such as Drysol, used for hyperhidrosis (excessive sweating). Dermatology sources describe topical aluminium chloride as a first-line treatment, in higher concentrations than ordinary antiperspirants, which typically use aluminium chlorohydrate . It acts as an astringent that reduces sweat output .

name: Sofpironium bromide (Sofdra)
summary: A prescription anticholinergic gel for underarm sweating, approved in Japan (2020) and the US (2024) - an approved sweat treatment, not a general looks product.
lead: Sofpironium bromide is a topical anticholinergic medication for primary axillary hyperhidrosis, excessive underarm sweating without an underlying medical cause. It was developed by Bodor Laboratories, licensed to Brickell Biotech (development code BBI-4000), and approved in Japan in 2020 as Ecclock and in the US in 2024 as Sofdra.

name: Zilpaterol (Zilmax)
summary: A beta-agonist cattle feed additive that grows lean beef; there are no human studies and no documented appearance use in the sources.
lead: Zilpaterol is a synthetic beta-2 adrenergic agonist given orally to cattle under the brand name Zilmax, produced by Merck's animal-health unit Intervet. It is fed during the last three to six weeks in a feedlot, with a withdrawal period before slaughter, to increase muscle mass and feed efficiency.

name: Ractopamine (Paylean)
summary: A beta-agonist livestock feed additive for lean pork and beef; no human appearance use is documented, though it matters in anti-doping.
lead: Ractopamine hydrochloride is a phenethanolamine beta-adrenergic agonist used as a feed additive in swine, cattle and turkeys to promote lean muscle growth and improve feed efficiency. Elanco Animal Health, formerly part of Eli Lilly, developed it.

name: Albuterol (Salbutamol)
summary: The standard asthma rescue inhaler; its use for fat loss or muscle is limited to scattered bodybuilder use and small lean-mass studies of oral dosing.
lead: Albuterol, known as salbutamol outside the US, is a short-acting beta-2 adrenergic agonist sold as Ventolin, ProAir and Proventil, among others. It is a first-line rescue bronchodilator for bronchospasm in asthma and COPD.

name: Terbutaline
summary: A prescription beta-2 agonist for asthma with an FDA boxed warning against use in preterm labour; no appearance trials exist.
lead: Terbutaline is a selective beta-2 adrenergic agonist sold as Bricanyl, Brethine and Marex, among other names. It was patented in 1966, entered medical use in 1970 and is indicated for preventing and reversing bronchospasm in people aged 12 and older with asthma, bronchitis and emphysema.

name: Rimonabant (Acomplia)
summary: A withdrawn prescription weight-loss pill that blocks the CB1 receptor; it produced weight loss in trials but was pulled in 2008 over depression and suicidality.
lead: Rimonabant, sold as Acomplia (and Zimulti), is an oral anti-obesity drug that blocks the cannabinoid-1 (CB1) receptor. It was developed by Sanofi-Aventis and was the first CB1 inverse agonist approved anywhere.

name: Lorcaserin (Belviq)
summary: An FDA-approved prescription weight-loss pill (Belviq) that modestly outperformed placebo in trials and was pulled in 2020 over a cancer signal.
lead: Lorcaserin, sold as Belviq, is a selective serotonin 5-HT2C receptor agonist that was prescribed for chronic weight management. It was developed by Arena Pharmaceuticals and approved by the US FDA in 2012.

name: Fenfluramine / phentermine (Fen-Phen)
summary: A 1990s prescription weight-loss drug pairing withdrawn in 1997 after heart valve damage and pulmonary hypertension were linked to it.
lead: Fen-phen is the informal name for the combination of the appetite suppressants fenfluramine and phentermine, which was prescribed for weight loss in the United States in the 1990s.  Fenfluramine mainly releases serotonin, while phentermine mainly releases norepinephrine.

name: Dexfenfluramine (Redux)
summary: The 1990s serotonin diet pill pulled from the market in 1997 after heart-valve and lung-pressure harms.
lead: Dexfenfluramine, sold in the United States under the brand name Redux, is the dextrorotatory enantiomer of fenfluramine and was developed as a serotonin-acting appetite suppressant for obesity. It is structurally related to amphetamine but is described as lacking amphetamine-type stimulant effects.

name: Phenylpropanolamine
summary: Former OTC decongestant and diet-pill stimulant pulled in the early 2000s after a hemorrhagic stroke link.
lead: Phenylpropanolamine (PPA) is a sympathomimetic drug related to ephedrine and amphetamine that was long used as a nasal decongestant and as an over-the-counter and prescription appetite suppressant. It was a common ingredient of cold remedies and diet aids.

name: Obetrol (amphetamine salts)
summary: The 1960s amphetamine-and-methamphetamine diet pill that became Adderall's ancestor.
lead: Obetrol was a prescription diet pill sold in the United States in the 1950s and 1960s by Obetrol Pharmaceuticals, a division of Rexar Pharmacal. It combined four amphetamine and methamphetamine salts and was marketed for exogenous obesity.

name: Cetilistat
summary: An orlistat-style fat-blocking pill with phase 2 data and limited availability outside Japan.
lead: Cetilistat (ATL-962) is a pancreatic lipase inhibitor developed as an anti-obesity drug. Like orlistat, it blocks intestinal enzymes that break down dietary fat, so some ingested fat is excreted rather than absorbed.

name: Plenity (Gelesis100)
summary: A swallowed gel capsule that swells in the stomach to promote fullness; cleared as a device with modest evidence.
lead: Plenity, developed as Gelesis100 by Gelesis, is an oral hydrogel taken in capsules before meals for weight management in adults with overweight or obesity. It is made of carboxymethylcellulose cross-linked with citric acid.

name: HU6
summary: An experimental, slow-release prodrug of the toxic fat-burner DNP, still in phase 2 trials.
lead: HU6 is an investigational once-daily oral drug from Rivus Pharmaceuticals. It is a prodrug of 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP), a mitochondrial uncoupler, and is designed to give more stable blood concentrations than DNP itself.

name: UBT251
summary: Investigational once-weekly GLP-1/GIP/glucagon triple agonist from China, licensed to Novo Nordisk; phase 2 data exist, but it is not an approved or prescribable drug.
lead: UBT251 is an investigational long-acting peptide that activates three receptors at once: the glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) and glucagon receptors. It was developed by United Biotechnology, a subsidiary of The United Laboratories International Holdings (TUL) in China, and is given as a once-weekly subcutaneous injection in trials.

name: Benzphetamine
summary: Old-school prescription amphetamine-type appetite suppressant labelled for a few weeks of use in obesity; Schedule III and not a cosmetic drug.
lead: Benzphetamine (brand name Didrex, among others) is a prescription sympathomimetic amine used as an appetite suppressant. In the United States it is labelled as a short-term adjunct, lasting a few weeks, to a calorie-restricted weight-reduction regimen for people with a body mass index of 30 kg/m2 or higher who have not responded to diet and exercise alone.

name: Phendimetrazine
summary: Older prescription stimulant appetite suppressant, a phenmetrazine prodrug, labelled for a few weeks of obesity treatment; controlled and not a cosmetic drug.
lead: Phendimetrazine (brand names include Bontril) is a prescription stimulant of the morpholine class used as an appetite suppressant. The US label indicates it as a short-term adjunct, lasting a few weeks, to a calorie-restricted regimen in patients with a body mass index of 30 kg/m2 or higher who have not responded to diet or exercise alone.

name: Diethylpropion
summary: Older prescription appetite suppressant labelled for a few weeks of obesity treatment; Schedule IV in the US and recommended for withdrawal in the EU.
lead: Diethylpropion, also called amfepramone, is a prescription appetite suppressant of the phenethylamine and cathinone families. The US label indicates it as a short-term adjunct, lasting a few weeks, to a calorie-restricted regimen for people with a body mass index of 30 kg/m2 or higher who have not responded to diet or exercise alone.

name: Pioglitazone
summary: Prescription diabetes drug that raises subcutaneous fat; appearance-related claims about it are untested in humans.
lead: Pioglitazone (brand name Actos) is an oral type 2 diabetes drug in the thiazolidinedione class. It was developed by Takeda, came into medical use in 1999 and is now generic.

name: Anamorelin
summary: Oral ghrelin-receptor drug studied for cancer cachexia; it raised lean mass in trials but has no appearance-use data.
lead: Anamorelin is an investigational oral drug that activates the ghrelin receptor (also called the growth hormone secretagogue receptor). It has been developed for cancer cachexia, the wasting syndrome of appetite loss, weight loss and muscle loss seen in advanced cancer. It also goes by the development codes ONO-7643 and RC-1291.

name: Macimorelin
summary: Oral ghrelin-receptor agonist approved only as a one-time diagnostic for adult GH deficiency; nothing on looks.
lead: Macimorelin (brand name Macrilen) is an orally active ghrelin-receptor agonist that stimulates release of growth hormone. It is approved by the US FDA as a diagnostic test for adult growth hormone deficiency (AGHD), not as a treatment.

name: Capromorelin
summary: Oral ghrelin agonist sold as a pet appetite stimulant; a human older-adult trial showed modest lean mass change and was not pursued.
lead: Capromorelin is an orally active ghrelin-receptor agonist and growth hormone secretagogue developed by Pfizer. It is approved for veterinary use, as Entyce for appetite stimulation in dogs (US, 2016) and Elura for weight loss in cats with chronic kidney disease (US, 2020).

name: Relamorelin
summary: Injected ghrelin analogue tested for diabetic gastroparesis; phase 3 trials were terminated and there is no appearance data.
lead: Relamorelin (RM-131) is a synthetic pentapeptide ghrelin analogue that is injected subcutaneously. It was developed to treat diabetic gastroparesis, a condition of delayed stomach emptying, and was also studied in constipation and anorexia nervosa.
